name: Continuous Batching and Model Serving
intent: Keep a GPU busy by running many requests through each decode step, letting finished sequences leave and new ones join at every step, and protect the service when demand exceeds what the GPU can do.
scenario: A chat service runs a model on a few GPU replicas behind a router. Answers range from 20 tokens to 400. With one request at a time a replica produces about 50 tokens/s and its arithmetic units sit mostly idle. With static batches, a 30 token answer waits in a batch with a 300 token one. The team moves to continuous batching with chunked prefill, paged KV blocks, a bounded queue and a load-aware router.
problem: A decode step is limited by how fast the GPU can read the model weights, not by arithmetic, so a step costs almost the same for 1 sequence or for 32. Serving one request at a time wastes most of the machine. Batching fixes that, but requests arrive at random times and want different numbers of tokens: a batch that must wait for its longest member holds short answers hostage and leaves slots empty, a long prompt can freeze everyone else's output, and reserving worst-case KV memory (the attention data the model keeps for every token so far) per request wastes most of the cache. On top of that, when demand exceeds capacity an unbounded queue turns every request into a slow one.

howItWorks.title: Why batching raises throughput
howItWorks.text: In decode, every step streams all the weights (for example 16 GB for an 8B model in 16-bit) from GPU memory to produce one token per sequence. That read is the dominant cost and it is the same whether the batch holds 1 or 32 sequences; only a small extra cost per sequence (its KV cache reads and a little arithmetic) is added. So step time grows slowly with batch size while tokens per step grow linearly. In this page's model a step costs 20 ms plus 1 ms per sequence: 1 sequence gives about 48 tokens/s, 16 give about 440. The ceiling comes from KV memory and eventually from compute; see llm-inference-and-kv-cache for the memory formula.

howItWorks.title: Static batching and its head-of-line problem
howItWorks.text: The simplest server collects up to N requests, runs them together and returns when the whole batch is done. Because output lengths differ (20 tokens versus 400), the batch lasts as long as its longest sequence. Finished sequences are padded: they keep occupying a slot and still cost compute, so the GPU spends most steps with idle slots, and a short request has latency set by someone else's long answer. New requests wait for the next batch even though slots are empty.

howItWorks.title: Continuous (iteration-level) batching
howItWorks.text: The scheduler runs once per decode step, not once per batch. When a sequence emits its stop token it leaves immediately and its answer is returned; if the queue is not empty, a new request takes the slot at the next step (its prompt is read in first, which is called prefill). The batch is therefore a rolling set. Slots stay full while there is a queue, short requests finish in time proportional to their own length, and throughput on mixed lengths is typically a small multiple (often 2x to 10x depending on length spread and load) of static batching on the same hardware.

howItWorks.title: Throughput versus latency, and chunked prefill
howItWorks.text: More sequences per step means more tokens per second but a slower step, so each user sees slower tokens: p95 latency (the time that 95% of requests beat) improves while the queue is the problem, then flattens and rises once the queue is empty and batches only add step time. Prefill makes it worse: a new 4,000 token prompt is processed in a burst that can occupy a step for hundreds of milliseconds, freezing every running user. Chunked prefill splits the prompt into pieces (for example 256 to 2,048 tokens) mixed into ordinary decode steps, so the longest step stays short and inter-token latency stays steady, at a small cost in time to first token for the long prompt and in total throughput.

howItWorks.title: Paged KV-cache memory
howItWorks.text: A sequence's KV cache grows by one token per step and its final length is unknown. Reserving a contiguous region for the maximum length per request wastes most memory (a 530 token chat in a 4,096 token reservation uses 13%) and fragments the pool. Paged allocation stores the cache in fixed-size blocks (commonly 16 tokens) taken from a free list and referenced through a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory. Waste is bounded to less than one block per sequence, finished sequences return blocks instantly, and shared prompt prefixes can share blocks. The number of free blocks is what the scheduler really admits against.

howItWorks.title: Admission control, queueing and replicas
howItWorks.text: Demand above capacity makes an unbounded queue grow without limit, and every request, including those that will time out anyway, gets slow. Production servers bound the queue (and the tokens in flight), reject with a fast 429 or 503 (busy) when it is full, and may preempt or swap out sequences when KV blocks run out. A router in front sends each request to the replica with the least work (queued plus running tokens, not just connections), because requests are far from equal; round-robin sends a long generation to a busy replica and ruins tail latency. Replicas are scaled on queue depth or KV utilisation, with a warm-up time of minutes to load weights.

pros: Several times the tokens per second per GPU, which is the main cost lever of self-hosted inference
Short requests no longer wait for someone else's long answer, so median latency drops sharply
Slots and KV blocks are reused every step, so utilisation stays high on mixed workloads
A bounded queue turns overload into fast rejections instead of unbounded latency
cons: Per-user token speed falls as the batch grows, so throughput and latency pull against each other
A scheduler running every step is complex, and bugs (starvation, preemption loops, block leaks) are hard to reproduce
Chunked prefill and paged blocks add tuning knobs (chunk size, block size, memory fraction)
Capacity is no longer a simple requests-per-second number; it depends on the mix of prompt and output lengths
whenToUse: Self-hosted LLM serving where request lengths vary and traffic is concurrent
Any decode-heavy workload where the GPU is under-utilised at batch size 1
Interactive products that need both good cost per token and predictable inter-token latency
whenNotToUse: Offline or bulk jobs with uniform lengths, where large static batches are simple and just as efficient
Low-traffic services where the queue is almost always empty, so batches never form and batching buys nothing
When you call a hosted API: the provider already does this and your lever is concurrency limits and retries
Very small models or CPU inference where the step is compute-bound and not memory-bound
pitfalls: Sizing max batch by throughput alone: the p95 inter-token latency target usually caps it lower
Admitting by request count instead of KV blocks and tokens, so a few long contexts exhaust memory and trigger preemption storms
An unbounded queue or a client timeout longer than the queue wait, so the GPU generates answers nobody is waiting for
Routing by round-robin or open connections when request cost varies by 20x
Cancelled or disconnected clients that keep their sequence running and their KV blocks held
Reading average tokens/s in a benchmark with uniform lengths and expecting it in production with a mixed workload

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends chat requests with a prompt and a stream of output tokens in return.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: Picks a replica by outstanding work and rejects when the fleet is full.

roles.label: Scheduler
roles.description: Runs every decode step: admits, preempts and retires sequences, and bounds the queue.

roles.label: GPU batch
roles.description: Executes one forward pass per step for all sequences in the running batch.

roles.label: KV block pool
roles.description: Fixed-size cache blocks handed to sequences as they grow and freed when they finish.

quiz.question: A chat service runs static batches of 8 requests. In one batch, seven answers need about 30 tokens and one needs 300. The short answers return late and most GPU slots sit idle for most of the batch. What does continuous batching change?
options: It raises the batch size, so more requests share each static batch.
It sorts incoming requests by expected output length so each batch holds similar sizes.
It moves long answers to a separate GPU so they stop blocking.
Each decode step, finished sequences leave and queued requests fill their slots.
quiz.explanation: Slots are reused every step, so a short request finishes in time proportional to its own length. Grouping by length helps a little but cannot predict output length well. A bigger static batch only makes the wait for the longest member longer.

quiz.question: Users see tokens stream every 30 ms, but whenever someone submits a 6,000 token document everybody's stream freezes for about 400 ms. Which change targets this?
options: Lower the maximum batch size so each decode step finishes sooner for every request.
Use chunked prefill, so the long prompt is processed in slices mixed into decode steps.
Use smaller KV blocks so the prompt's cache is allocated faster during the burst.
Raise the maximum batch size so the prompt becomes a smaller share of each step's total work.
quiz.explanation: The freeze is one step swollen by the prompt burst. Chunked prefill keeps the longest step short, at a small cost to that prompt's time to first token. Changing batch size or block size does not shorten the burst.

quiz.question: Traffic doubles to twice the cluster's capacity. The queue is unbounded, clients time out after 30 seconds, and queue wait has grown to 90 seconds. GPUs are at 100 percent, yet almost no user gets an answer. What is the best fix?
options: Bound the queue and reject with a fast 429 when full, so admitted requests finish in time.
Raise the client timeout to 120 seconds so the queued work is not wasted.
Make the queue larger so that bursts are absorbed rather than rejected during peaks.
Raise the maximum batch size so the backlog drains faster.
quiz.explanation: The GPU is busy generating answers for clients that already gave up. Rejecting early keeps latency bounded for the requests that are accepted. A longer timeout or a larger queue only hides the overload, and a bigger batch slows every token.
